exam: A 58‑year‑old hypertensive man presents with right‑sided weakness 2 h after onset – what is your immediate management? — Assess FAST, obtain CT, consider IV alteplase if no bleed.
How does the NIH Stroke Scale guide treatment decisions? — Scores ≥6 suggest moderate‑severe stroke; higher scores may prompt thrombectomy evaluation.
A patient with sickle cell disease has sudden left‑sided weakness – which additional cause should you consider? — Cerebral vasculopathy from sickle cell, treat with exchange transfusion if confirmed.
Why is thrombolysis contraindicated in a patient on warfarin with INR 2.0? — INR >1.7 increases bleeding risk; avoid alteplase.
What bedside test helps differentiate stroke from hypoglycaemia? — Perform a rapid finger‑stick glucose; treat <70 mg/dL immediately.
In a setting without CT, what clinical features would make you defer thrombolysis? — Any suspicion of intracranial bleed (head trauma, anticoagulant use, uncontrolled hypertension).
Explain why statins are started after an ischemic stroke. — They stabilise plaques, reduce recurrent events, and improve endothelial function.
What are the key steps in preventing aspiration in an acute stroke patient? — Assess swallow, keep head elevated, consider NG tube only if safe.
ai.title: Ischemic Stroke
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Sudden focal neurological deficit caused by cerebral arterial occlusion. Prompt recognition, imaging, and reperfusion are essential to limit brain injury, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Accounts for ~80% of all strokes
Time‑dependent: neurons die within minutes of complete occlusion
sections.p: An ischemic stroke occurs when a cerebral artery is blocked, depriving brain tissue of oxygen and glucose. In East Africa, atherosclerosis, hypertension, and cardio‑embolism (including rheumatic heart disease) are common causes.

b: FAST: Face droop, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call help
NIHSS ≥6 predicts moderate‑to‑severe stroke
CT non‑contrast rules out hemorrhage; CT‑angiography identifies large‑vessel occlusion
sections.p: Diagnosis rests on the FAST exam, NIH Stroke Scale, and imaging. Severity is staged by the NIHSS and by imaging (CT/MRI) into early (<6 h), sub‑acute (6‑24 h), and late phases.

b: Within 4.5 h: IV alteplase if no contraindications
Within 6 h for large‑vessel occlusion: mechanical thrombectomy if available
Blood pressure control, glucose optimisation, and antiplatelet therapy are essential
sections.p: Early reperfusion (thrombolysis or thrombectomy) dramatically improves outcome. In low‑resource hospitals, lack of CT may force treatment decisions on clinical criteria alone.

t.b: Is the stroke hemorrhagic? – A hyperdense area indicates bleed; a normal scan supports ischemia
Is there a large‑vessel occlusion? – Shows site of blockage, guides thrombectomy
Is the patient hypoglycaemic? – Low glucose can mimic stroke; treat if <70 mg/dL
Are there contraindications to thrombolysis? – Low platelets, INR >1.7, or active bleed

b: Mechanical thrombectomy for M1 or ICA occlusion – if expertise and device present
Statin therapy for all ischemic stroke patients
Control BP <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis; target 140‑160 mmHg thereafter
Manage dysphagia, prevent aspiration, and monitor for cerebral edema
sections.p: Reperfusion, secondary prevention, and supportive care.

b: Hemorrhagic stroke – needs blood pressure lowering, no thrombolysis
Seizure with post‑ictal paralysis (Todd’s paresis) – resolves within hours
Migraine aura – gradual onset, visual symptoms predominate
sections.p: Conditions that cause acute focal deficits but require different treatment.

b: Normal CT within 3 h does not exclude early ischemia; rely on clinical timing
Mild hyperglycaemia can mask stroke severity on NIHSS
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

b: Always assess FAST first, then NIHSS
If CT unavailable but patient meets strict time and clinical criteria, some protocols allow thrombolysis
Identify cardio‑embolic sources (e.g., rheumatic mitral stenosis) in young patients
